study.research_problem: Conventional screw-type dental implants are not tailored to an individual extraction socket, and stress transmitted through the bone-implant interface depends on implant geometry and bone quality. A root-analog implant may improve anatomical fit, but porous regions can also concentrate stress when the solid core is removed.
study.exact_gap: Stress behavior of customized root-analog implants across Lekholm-Zarb bone densities and different porous-core configurations was poorly characterized. The study compares three customized RAI designs with a stock screw implant under matched FE loads, then checks the printed geometry and socket fit of one design.
study.objective_or_hypothesis: Use FEA to map von Mises stress in cortical bone, cancellous bone, and the implant for four bone-density types and four implant designs, and test whether porous RAI designs produce a more favorable stress pattern than a conventional screw implant without exceeding reported bone or titanium ultimate-strength limits.
study.study_design: Original computational implant-biomechanics study. A mandibular right second premolar from CBCT was converted to CAD; designs A (solid RAI), B (600 micrometre porous surface with a 2 mm solid core), C (porous surface without the core), and D (5 x 13 mm stock screw implant) were modeled in type I-IV rectangular bone boundaries. Isotropic homogeneous linear-elastic FE models applied 200 N vertical plus 40 N buccolingual horizontal force with fixed outer boundaries. Design B was laser powder-bed fused, tapped into a type-I polyurethane Sawbone socket, and micro-CT compared CAD-to-printed fit. The print check validates geometry/fit only, not FE stresses, osseointegration, or clinical outcomes.
study.sample_or_model: One CBCT-derived right second premolar had original dimensions 7.3 mm buccolingual, 5.0 mm mesiodistal, and 14.7 mm root length; the modeled remaining root was 6.93 x 4.48 mm and 12.25 mm long. Design B used a 2 mm-deep, 600 micrometre pore macrostructure below the coronal 4 mm with a 2 mm solid core; design C removed that core. The bone block was 23.31 mm high, 10.5 mm buccolingual, and 5 mm mesiodistal from the shoulder. Type I was cortical only; type II had 2 mm cortical plus normal cancellous bone; type III had 1 mm cortical plus normal cancellous bone; type IV had 1 mm cortical plus low-density cancellous bone. All FE materials were isotropic, homogeneous, linear elastic and assumed fully osseointegrated with all porous spaces filled by bone.
comparators: Design A solid root-analog, B porous surface with solid core, C porous surface without core, and D conventional stock screw implant
Lekholm-Zarb type I, II, III, and IV bone-density boundary models
Cortical-bone, cancellous-bone, and implant von Mises stress
FE CAD design versus LPBF-printed design B geometry and socket fit
Predicted stress versus reported ultimate tolerance of approximately 100 MPa cortical bone, 8 MPa cancellous bone, and 900 MPa titanium
method_spine: Generate a CBCT premolar CAD model and define solid, porous-core, porous-no-core, and stock screw designs (S003:C01-S004:C01).
Construct rectangular type I-IV bone boundaries with cortical/cancellous thickness and density states, then assign isotropic material properties and full osseointegration (S005:C01-S006:C01).

Apply simultaneous 200 N vertical and 40 N horizontal abutment loads with fixed mesial/distal boundaries and compute cortical, cancellous, and implant von Mises stresses for all 16 combinations (S006:C01; S008:C01).
Compare design-specific stress patterns with reported ultimate stress limits and identify the porous-core trade-off (S009:C01-S011:C01).
LPBF-print design B, machine/tap a type-I polyurethane socket, micro-CT scan the assembly, and quantify discrepancy/RMSE across 344,016 surface elements (S007:C01; S012:C01).
Interpret stress and geometry results within explicit FEA, contact, anisotropy, loading, fit, and biological limitations (S013:C01-S013:C02; S014:C01).

verification: The FE analysis is a comparative 16-case setup with stated loads, constraints, material assumptions, and stress outputs; no mesh-convergence, contact-convergence, or code-verification result is reported (S006:C01; S008:C01).
Micro-CT and RMS element distributions verify CAD-to-LPBF geometric fidelity and socket fit for design B, not the stress solution (S007:C01; S012:C01).
calibration: Bone and implant material properties and ultimate stress tolerances are taken from prior literature; no patient-specific density calibration or printed-material mechanical calibration is performed (S006:C01; S009:C01-S011:C01).
The 200/40 N load pair and full osseointegration assumption are prescribed boundary conditions, not calibrated to this patient's mastication or measured interface contact.
validation: The only physical validation is LPBF geometry/fit of design B in a type-I polyurethane block, with mean RMS approximately 0.09 mm and most elements within 0.10 mm; no experimental stress, strain, fracture, or interface-micromotion validation is present (S007:C01; S012:C01).
The paper's stress ranking is therefore a model comparison and its clinical interpretation remains prospective (S013:C02).
sensitivity: The explicit computational comparison spans four bone-density categories and four implant configurations, exposing the effect of a solid core and low-density cancellous bone (S005:C01; S008:C01-S011:C01).
No sensitivity is reported for anisotropy, partial bone contact, friction, implant orientation, masticatory force histories, material uncertainty, pore size, or manufacturing defects.
application_prediction: Lower modeled stress for RAI designs, especially design B in type-IV cancellous bone, predicts a potentially favorable mechanical pattern; it does not demonstrate osseointegration, reduced bone loss, or clinical success (S009:C01-S014:C01).
Porosity may increase surface area and mechanical interlocking in future use, but the paper does not measure tissue ingrowth or interface strength (S013:C01-S013:C02).

primary_outcomes: Sixteen FE combinations (four bone models x four designs) were analyzed. Cortical-bone stress was highest at the implant shoulder for types II-IV; design A generally had the lowest cortical stress and design C the highest, while all were below the cited approximately 100 MPa cortical ultimate tolerance (S008:C01-S009:C01).

Cancellous-bone stresses were below the cited 8 MPa ultimate strength except design C in type III bone. Design B had the lowest cancellous stress in type-IV bone, whereas design D exceeded designs A and C in the reported comparison (S010:C01).
Implant stresses were lowest for design A and highest for design C across bone types, with all below the cited approximately 900 MPa titanium ultimate tolerance (S011:C01).

The design-B LPBF implant was placed in a type-I polyurethane foam socket. Micro-CT showed a 0.05-0.10 mm vertical discrepancy; across 344,016 elements, mean RMS was 0.09 mm, with 236,817 elements at 0-0.10 mm, 93,362 at 0.10-0.20 mm, 11,323 at 0.20-0.30 mm, 2,423 at 0.30-0.40 mm, and 91 at 0.40-0.50 mm (S007:C01; S012:C01).

The paper interprets the no-core porous design C as stress-concentrating at strut edges and considers A/B safer than C/D under the stated stress thresholds, while noting that an equivalent stress near 1.6 MPa has been associated in prior canine work with preventing crestal bone loss; that latter result is external evidence, not this study's endpoint (S013:C01).
The study reports no numeric stress uncertainty, independent specimens for the FE comparison, fatigue cycles, measured bone contact, or biological/clinical response.
study.highest_evidence_level_reached: Comparative FE stress prediction for one CBCT-derived premolar across four idealized bone-density models and four implant designs, with one-design LPBF geometry/fit verification in a type-I polyurethane block. No stress/strain experiment, partial-contact model, biological ingrowth, fatigue, or clinical validation is reached.

argument_map.central_claim: A customized root-analog implant with a porous surface and retained solid core can show a more favorable modeled stress pattern than a stock screw implant across simplified bone-density states, whereas removing the core concentrates stress; the claim is a bounded FE design hypothesis, not evidence of clinical osseointegration or outcome improvement.
data: CBCT-derived anatomy and four CAD implant designs provide a controlled geometry comparison (S003:C01-S004:C01).
Sixteen FE cases vary bone density and implant design under matched 200 N/40 N loading, with cortical, cancellous, and implant stress comparisons (S005:C01-S011:C01).
One LPBF-printed design B is checked for CAD-to-socket geometry, with exact RMS counts and discrepancy ranges, but no stress measurement (S007:C01; S012:C01).
argument_map.warrant: Retaining a solid core can distribute load away from sharp internal strut edges, while a porous surface may increase nominal contact area and future ingrowth opportunity; stress safety in a simplified FE model still requires biological and interface evidence.
backing: Design A has the lowest modeled stress and design C the highest across several bone types, consistent with the core-removal mechanism (S009:C01-S011:C01).
Design B is selected for the physical print because its geometry is more complex yet printable and its fit error is concentrated away from the outer contact surface (S012:C01-S013:C01).
The discussion explicitly acknowledges that full contact, isotropy, fixed boundaries, and static loads differ from living oral tissues and parafunctional loading (S013:C02).
argument_map.qualifier: Stress values and safety comparisons apply to one CBCT anatomy, idealized homogeneous isotropic bone, full osseointegration, fixed outer boundaries, simultaneous 200 N/40 N loads, and the cited ultimate-strength thresholds. The printed fit check does not validate stress or tissue response.
rebuttals_or_boundaries: FE cannot predict bone response or ingrowth, and the laboratory validation cannot simulate porous bone formation (S013:C02).
Actual bone-to-implant contact may be 50-60% rather than the modeled full tie, and masticatory force magnitude/direction/duration vary across patients and parafunctions (S013:C02).
The stock implant is similar but not identical in size to the premolar root, and design C's high stress is sensitive to the no-core strut geometry (S013:C01-S013:C02).
Macro-porosity is not micro-roughness; L-PBF roughness can be 4-14 micrometres and surfaces above 2 micrometres may carry peri-implantitis trade-offs (S013:C01).

measured: CBCT/micro-CT dimensions, printed design-B geometry discrepancy, RMS distribution over 344,016 elements, and Sawbone socket placement are measured physical/manufacturing outcomes (S003:C01; S007:C01; S012:C01).
The paper reports no measured implant stress, bone strain, bone contact fraction, osseointegration, fatigue, or clinical outcome.
predicted: All cortical, cancellous, and implant von Mises stresses for 16 design-density combinations are FE predictions under full osseointegration and isotropic linear-elastic material assumptions (S006:C01; S008:C01-S011:C01).

Statements that porous RAI may reduce stress, improve mechanical interlocking, or support long-term clinical outcomes are application predictions or external-literature extrapolations (S013:C01-S013:C02; S014:C01).
inferred: The solid core in design B is inferred to reduce the strut-edge concentration seen in coreless design C, while preserving some macro-porous surface area (S013:C01).

A 0.05-0.10 mm fit discrepancy and mean RMS 0.09 mm are inferred to indicate acceptable manufacturing fit according to a cited threshold, but they do not establish contact mechanics during mastication (S012:C01-S013:C01).
Lower stress is inferred to be mechanically safer relative to cited ultimate limits, but fatigue, biological response, and bone-remodeling endpoints remain untested.
recommended: Validate FE stress and strain with instrumented or digital-image-correlation tests, partial-contact/friction models, patient-specific material density, and realistic mastication histories.
Quantify as-built pore/strut geometry, micro-roughness, residual stress, surface chemistry, and fatigue under relevant dental loading for multiple printed implants.
Measure bone-to-implant contact, tissue ingrowth, micromotion, peri-implant inflammation, and long-term function in appropriate preclinical and clinical studies.
Compare the stock control with identical outer dimensions and perform sensitivity to anisotropy, contact fraction, implant orientation, and parafunctional loading.
proxy_to_outcome_bridges: Von Mises stress below an ultimate-strength threshold is a static model proxy; it does not establish fatigue life, fracture probability, or clinical survival.
A CAD-to-print RMS fit error and tapped Sawbone placement validate geometry/fit, not osseointegration, bone quality response, or load transfer in vivo.
Macro-porosity and predicted contact area may enable ingrowth, but no cells, bone, histology, or interface mechanics were measured.
Modeled full osseointegration is a boundary assumption, not evidence that the implant achieved 100% bone contact.
overclaim_risks: The abstract's favorable stress statement and conclusion may be read as clinical safety even though only FE and geometry-fit validation were performed (S001:C01; S014:C01).

All FE materials are isotropic, homogeneous, linear elastic and fully osseointegrated; these assumptions can hide local anisotropy, contact gaps, stress peaks, and biological remodeling (S006:C01; S013:C02).
Using external 1.6 MPa crestal-bone and 100/8/900 MPa thresholds as if they were validated patient-specific limits risks false precision (S009:C01-S013:C01).
A single printed design B and one Sawbone type-I block do not establish manufacturing variability, fatigue durability, or performance in types II-IV bone.

section_moves.move: Frame customization and stress transfer as coupled design problems, then state the density/design comparison and validation boundary.
section_moves.execution: The introduction contrasts stock screw implants with root-analog customization, explains bone-density and interface-stress drivers, and identifies sparse RAI evidence before stating the FEA objective (S002:C01).
section_moves.transferable_principle: End an implant introduction with the exact anatomy, design variants, comparator, loading, and endpoint rather than a generic promise of personalization.
section_moves.failure_mode: Presenting anatomic fit as clinical superiority before evaluating bone quality, interface contact, and failure endpoints conflates geometry with outcome.

section_moves.move: Make each material/geometry/contact state explicit before interpreting FE stress.
section_moves.execution: The methods separately define CBCT-to-CAD dimensions, solid-core versus coreless porosity, type I-IV cortical/cancellous boundaries, full osseointegration, isotropic linear elasticity, fixed boundaries, and 200/40 N loads (S003:C01-S006:C01).
section_moves.transferable_principle: For an implant FE study, state nominal design, tissue state, contact state, material law, load history, and boundary conditions as separate evidence fields.
section_moves.failure_mode: A fully tied and fully osseointegrated porous model can be mistaken for an as-implanted or partially integrated interface.

section_moves.move: Report design-by-bone-density stress patterns before declaring a preferred porous design.
section_moves.execution: Results separate cortical, cancellous, and implant stresses across all 16 combinations, preserving the type-III design-C exception and type-IV design-B cancellous advantage (S008:C01-S011:C01).
section_moves.transferable_principle: When a design's ranking changes with tissue state, report the interaction rather than one whole-study winner.
section_moves.failure_mode: Averaging bone types can hide the coreless design's cancellous-bone exceedance and the type-IV benefit of design B.

section_moves.move: Label printed geometry/fit as a limited validation layer and state what remains unvalidated.
section_moves.execution: The paper reports design-B LPBF fabrication, tapped Sawbone placement, micro-CT discrepancy, and RMS element counts, then acknowledges that this cannot reproduce bone ingrowth or tissue response (S007:C01; S012:C01; S013:C02).
section_moves.transferable_principle: Name the physical quantity tested by a validation experiment and stop the validation claim at that quantity.
section_moves.failure_mode: Calling a geometry RMS check model validation can make a stress prediction appear experimentally confirmed.

section_moves.move: Place porous-surface potential beside full-contact, anisotropy, loading, roughness, and biological limitations.
section_moves.execution: The discussion states that porosity may increase interlocking but preserves the FEA limitations, 50-60% real contact possibility, isotropic simplification, variable mastication, non-identical stock control, and micro-roughness/peri-implantitis boundary (S013:C01-S013:C02).
section_moves.transferable_principle: A design implication should be accompanied by the interface, material, loading, and biological assumptions that could reverse it.
section_moves.failure_mode: Macro-porosity can be written as proven osseointegration if surface roughness and actual bone contact are not separated.

author_reported: FE cannot predict living-tissue response, and the laboratory print validation cannot simulate bone ingrowth in pores (S013:C02).
Masticatory force magnitude, direction, and duration vary, particularly with parafunction; the model uses one simultaneous 200 N/40 N load pair (S013:C02).
Full tight contact was assumed even though histology can show 50-60% bone-to-implant contact, and bone was simplified as isotropic/homogeneous (S013:C02).
The stock implant is similar but not identical to the premolar-root dimensions, and micro-roughness is not represented by FEA (S013:C01-S013:C02).
reader_identified: One CBCT anatomy and one printed design B provide no anatomical, manufacturing, or patient-level replicate variability.
No FE mesh convergence, contact sensitivity, material calibration, or uncertainty interval is reported, despite very small reported fit errors and stress-threshold comparisons.
The physical model is type-I polyurethane only, so the geometry/fit check does not test types II-IV cancellous states or mechanical stress transfer.
The model assumes all porous spaces are filled with bone and does not resolve staged ingrowth, immature tissue, frictional micromotion, degradation, fatigue, or peri-implant inflammation.
The four design stress rankings depend on the chosen 600 micrometre porous depth, solid-core thickness, stock-implant size, and fixed boundaries; no pore-size or geometry sensitivity is given.
likely_bias_direction: Full osseointegration and tied contact likely smooth or increase load transfer relative to an early implant state, while fixed boundaries may concentrate stress at the model block edges.
Isotropic homogeneous bone and one static load pair may understate patient-specific anisotropy, parafunctional peaks, and orientation effects.
Using a type-I Sawbone for geometry validation may favor apparent fit and does not represent weaker type-IV cancellous bone.
The stock control's non-identical geometry and the selected design B for printing may bias comparisons toward design-specific rather than matched-volume effects.
limitations.scope_boundary: The study supports comparative static FE hypotheses about four RAI/stock geometries under four simplified bone-density states, plus design-B LPBF fit accuracy in a type-I polyurethane socket. It does not establish stress measurement, fatigue durability, partial-contact mechanics, bone ingrowth, peri-implant health, or clinical superiority.

writing_capability_candidates.capability: Treat anatomy, porous-core geometry, bone-density state, interface contact, and loading as separate FE state variables before comparing stress.
writing_capability_candidates.manuscript_use: Implant FE methods, design matrix, interaction Results, and model audit.
writing_capability_candidates.counterexample_or_boundary: Full osseointegration and isotropic homogeneous materials do not represent early or heterogeneous living-tissue contact; rankings remain model-specific.

writing_capability_candidates.capability: Use design-by-tissue-state interaction tables and preserve exceptions rather than reporting one global porous-implant winner.
writing_capability_candidates.manuscript_use: Results matrix, comparator fairness, and design selection rationale.
writing_capability_candidates.counterexample_or_boundary: Design C is the highest-stress case and exceeds the cited cancellous limit in type III, while design B is lowest in type-IV cancellous bone; a single average would conceal this interaction.

writing_capability_candidates.capability: Limit manufacturing validation claims to the physical quantity tested—CAD-to-print geometry and fit—before discussing stress, fixation, or osseointegration.
writing_capability_candidates.manuscript_use: Validation section, nominal-to-as-built audit, and translational boundary.
writing_capability_candidates.counterexample_or_boundary: A 0.09 mm RMS geometry result in a type-I polyurethane block does not validate implant stress or tissue ingrowth in type-II-IV living bone.

writing_capability_candidates.capability: Bridge macro-porosity to a future biological hypothesis while explicitly separating micro-roughness, contact fraction, stress, and clinical endpoints.
writing_capability_candidates.manuscript_use: Discussion, mechanistic interpretation, and recommendation language.
writing_capability_candidates.counterexample_or_boundary: The study measures neither bone contact nor micro-roughness response; porosity and static stress cannot be written as proven osseointegration or reduced peri-implantitis.

critical_weaknesses: A single CBCT anatomy, idealized isotropic full-contact models, and one static load pair limit generalizability.
LPBF validation measures geometry/fit only in type-I polyurethane and does not validate stress, contact, fatigue, or ingrowth.
No mesh/contact/material sensitivity, numerical uncertainty, fatigue, or biological endpoint is reported.
External ultimate-stress and crestal-bone thresholds are used as proxies rather than patient-specific validated limits.

summary_zh: 这是一项基于单个 CBCT 下颌第二前磨牙的原始 FE 设计比较研究。四种设计为实心根形植入物 A、带 600 μm 多孔表面且保留 2 mm 实心核心的 B、无核心多孔 C，以及尺寸相近但不完全相同的库存螺纹植入物 D；四种骨状态为 Lekholm–Zarb I–IV。模型假设均质各向同性线弹性骨、完全骨整合，施加 200 N 垂直+40 N 颊舌向载荷。16 组 FE 结果显示设计 C 在若干骨状态应力最高，设计 B 在 IV 型松质骨应力最低，模型应力与文献给出的约 100 MPa 皮质骨、8 MPa 松质骨和 900 MPa 钛极限比较。B 通过 L-PBF 打印并在 I 型聚氨酯 Sawbone 中微 CT 检查，平均 RMS 约 0.09 mm、344016 个元素给出完整分布；这只验证几何/贴合，不验证应力或骨长入。实际接触比例、咀嚼载荷、各向异性、微粗糙、疲劳、微动、组织和临床端点均未测量，静态应力安全不能直接写成临床优势。
reader_notes: Primary Luna reader reviewed all 15 non-reference packet chunks in exact order: S001:C01; S002:C01; S003:C01; S004:C01; S005:C01; S006:C01; S007:C01; S008:C01; S009:C01; S010:C01; S011:C01; S012:C01; S013:C01-S013:C02; S014:C01.

Full-text adjudication classifies the article as original FE design comparison with one-design LPBF geometry/fit validation. It is not a biological, fatigue, or clinical validation study despite the abstract's prospective language.

The card retains all four designs, bone-density states, loads, material/contact assumptions, stress-limit units, geometry RMSE counts, and the design-C/type-III exception; no stress value is invented where the packet reports only relative ranking.

The validation firewall is explicit: a 0.09 mm CAD-to-print RMS in a type-I polyurethane socket validates manufacturing geometry/fit only, while stress, bone response, osseointegration, fatigue, and clinical outcomes remain predicted or unmeasured.
